newsitem.title: POLAND: POLISH RIGHT PLEASED WITH NARROW CONSTITUTION VOTE.
newsitem.headline: POLISH RIGHT PLEASED WITH NARROW CONSTITUTION VOTE.

text.p: Poland's rightist opposition failed to block a new constitution backed by the ruling ex-communists, but on Monday it hailed the narrow verdict in the referendum as a boost for its election hopes.
Exit polls, released after Sunday's nationwide vote, showed 56.8 percent backed the constitution and 43.2 percent opposed it, in turnout of 39.8 percent of the 28 million voters.
Official results were due late on Monday or on Tuesday.

"It turned out the constitution gained the acceptance of only about 20 percent of society. This is a yellow card shown to the government," said Tomasz Tywonek, spokesman of the Solidarity Election Action (AWS) alliance.

The AWS, grouping more than 30 rightist parties around the Solidarity union, had opposed the constitution drafted by the ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) with its Peasant allies partners and two parliamentary opposition parties.
Many analysts saw the vote as a test for elections around September when the AWS, weak in parliament, hopes to win power.

Opinion polls have long shown the AWS and SLD about level, well ahead of other parties, with between a fifth and a quarter of votes each and a survey among referendum voters also by the PBS polling institute showed them with 22.6 and 22.3 percent.
Under Poland's electoral system this would translate into about a third of the seats each in the 460-member parliament in which the ruling coalition now has about two-thirds of seats.
President Aleksander Kwasniewski, an ex-communist, said the verdict would not have a direct bearing on the election.
"I don't think we can say today who will win," he told public television after the referendum result, adding that he was unpleasantly surprised by the low turnout.
The ex-communist leader Jozef Oleksy said he was satisfied, especially as in his view the right misrepresented the issues and politicised them rather than focussing on concrete matters.
But Solidarity's Tywonek told Reuters that with slim resources the right had changed opinion poll results of a month ago showing far greater support for the constitution.
"It shows we can conduct a good campaign," he said.

He said that while the president and prime minister had spoken on television and used the state apparatus to promote the constitution, its opponents had relied on leafleting and publicly-funded election broadcasts.

He also said the centrist opposition Union for Freedom (UW), which is descended like Solidarity from the pre-1989 struggle for democracy but backed the constitution, would be wise to shun future cooperation with the ex-communists.
"Above all for the UW this is a signal to alter its attitudes. This constitution coalition, which could in future be a possible government coalition, got very small support."
Solidarity leaders argued the constitution betrayed national interests by allowing Poland to surrender by treaty some functions to international organisations.
Appealing to strongly pro-Catholic, patriotic voters it also argued that the constitution did not clearly invoke God and include a clause banning abortion, now legal in Poland.
The constitution's backers said the document, designed to enshrine liberties won with the fall of communism, is Western style and embraces people of all faiths or none.

If the exit poll results are confirmed the new charter takes effect in just more than three months, but AWS and its sister rightist party the Movement for the Reconstruction of Poland have vowed to change it if they win the election.

The head of the public CBOS institute, Janusz Durlik confirmed that polls had showed anti-constitution sentiment gaining sharply and even a week ago 47 percent of intending voters had been for, 22 against and 31 undecided.

He said voters, though largely not tied to specific parties, had decided in the vote along electoral loyalties stemming from pre-1989 splits rather than backing centrist opposition hopes the constitution would build consensus.

"People saw this as a warm-up for the election and in recent polls they said the...constitutional referendum is stoking up a sharp election debate and the constitution would not be an element of consensus," he said. -- Warsaw Newsroom +48 22 653 9700
